title: What the homepage has to prove for a developer-tool company
metaTitle: What a developer-tool homepage must prove
excerpt: An engineer skeptical of marketing needs a real screen of the tool and a way to try it. A slogan about empowering developers does not survive that read.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen. The article is about skipping the empty approach and showing the tool itself.
caption: A long approach is the wrong hero when the tool should be in the first view. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a developer-tool homepage show first?
faqs.answer: Show a real screen, transcript, or snippet of the tool doing its job, and a way to try it without a meeting. Name the object the tool touches, such as a pull request, a query, or a test. Leave slogans about empowering developers off the first view.

faqs.question: Should the only call to action be a demo?
faqs.answer: No, if the tool can be tried. A sandbox, an install command, or a short quickstart should be the first path. A demo can exist for procurement or a security review, and it should be labeled as that, not as the only door.

faqs.question: How do you test the homepage with an engineer?
faqs.answer: Give someone who did not build the page about ten seconds, then ask what the tool does and how to try it. Let them try. If the path ends in a sales email, the page overpromised. Change the path until a stranger can produce the tool's real output.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results
How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A developer-tool company homepage has to convince an engineer who is skeptical of marketing. Show a real screen of the tool, and offer a way to try the product. Do both in the first view. If they can tell what the tool does to a file, a request, or a log, and they can reach a working trial without a meeting, the page has done its job.

A slogan about empowering developers fails this buyer. They have shipped code this week. They do not need to be empowered by a headline. They need to see the interface, the command, or the diff your tool actually produces, and a path that lets them run it on something of their own.

## Write for the person who will use it

The reader is often the user and the skeptic in one. They may need a manager's approval later. The homepage still has to survive their private read. They will open docs if the tool looks real. They will close the tab if the page sounds like a poster.

Name the object the tool touches. A pull request. A query. A flaky test. A log line. "The future of developer experience" names nothing they can point at. "Shows the query plan next to the slow endpoint" names a job. Use the second kind of sentence, in the words they already type.

Assume they know what a terminal is. Do not teach the industry. Do not open with a history of software complexity. Spend the first lines on the screen and the try path. Save the company for an about page they may never need if the tool is good.

They may arrive from a recommendation, a changelog, or a search for the error your tool claims to catch. Meet that arrival. The first sentence should still make sense if they have no patience for a brand. A homepage that requires the campaign to explain it is a homepage that lost.

## Put a real screen in the first view

Show the tool as it looks when it is working. A trace. A review comment. A CLI transcript with a real command and a real result. Crop so the important line is readable. You can use sample data. You should not draw a fictional interface that the product does not ship.

Put the command or the screen where a cold visit sees it without scrolling. The headline and the artifact should agree. If the line says the tool flags a risky migration, the artifact should show that flag, not an abstract dashboard of health scores.

If the product is a library, the artifact can be a short snippet and the result of running it. Keep it short enough to read. Link to the full example in the docs. The homepage is the proof, not the manual. Three lines that run beat thirty lines that perform completeness.

Google's Core Web Vitals guidance treats the largest content on screen as something that should paint quickly. A good Largest Contentful Paint is within 2.5 seconds of the page starting to load. When the real screen is that content, a late image is a late product. Engineers notice waiting. They interpret it as a hint about everything else you ship.

## Trying the product is the action

One action should try the product. "Run it" or "Open a sandbox" or "Install" can be right if they are true. "Request a demo" as the only door fails the buyer who came to touch the tool. A demo can exist for procurement. It should not be the first and only path.

Make the try path short. A sandbox in the browser. A package install with a copyable command. A free project with no card, if that is honest. Tell them what they will get in the next minute. A sample repo. A token that expires. A local run with no account. Surprise accounts are how trials die.

Label the button with the mechanism. "Create a sandbox." "Copy the install command." "Read the quickstart" is acceptable only if the quickstart reaches a result in a few steps. "Get started" is too vague for this reader. They want to know whether getting started is a download or a sales form.

If a paid tier is required for the real job, say what the free try includes and where it stops. A sandbox that hides the core feature is a brochure. Let them feel the job, and name the limit beside the button. Engineers prefer a fence to a maze.

## The slogan they have learned to ignore

"Empowering developers" can sit on any company that sells to people who write code. It does not say what happens when they run the tool. The same is true of "delightful developer experience," "blazing fast," and "built for builders." These lines are comfortable in a workshop. They are empty on a homepage.

Replace the slogan with the mechanism. What the tool reads. What it writes. What it refuses to do. "Comments on the pull request when a migration locks a table" is a mechanism. It is also a sentence an engineer can falsify by trying the product. Slogans cannot be falsified, which is why this buyer distrusts them.

You can keep a point of view after the mechanism. Quiet tools. Strict defaults. No telemetry without a switch. Those are positions. They belong under the screen, as sentences, not above it as a banner. The banner is the job.

Read the line next to the artifact before you approve it. Cover the picture and see whether the words still name an object. Cover the words and see whether the picture still shows that object. If either side can be swapped for another tool's homepage, you are still in slogan territory. Swap in the mechanism and look again. The test takes a minute. It saves a redesign later, when someone has already built a campaign around a line the product cannot prove.

If a campaign line is already printed on a wall, leave it on the wall. The homepage has a different duty. It has to survive a reader who is hostile to campaigns. Give that reader the artifact.

## Order the page around the trial

Use an order that respects a skeptical read.

1. The job, in one sentence, with the object it touches.
2. A real screen, transcript, or snippet.
3. A way to try the product, with the limit stated.
4. Two facts that change the decision. Latency behavior. Where it runs. What it does not collect.
5. A short proof. One constraint, one decision, one picture. Not a logo wall.
6. The try path again, for the person who scrolled to be sure.

Docs can be linked. They should not replace step two. An engineer will open docs after they believe the tool exists. The homepage's job is to create that belief with evidence, then get out of the way.

Nielsen Norman Group's review of how long people stay on pages is blunt. Users often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds are when they decide whether to stay. The snippet and the try path have to fit that window. The company story will not.

## What the homepage should not borrow from a SaaS brochure

Do not lead with a customer logo bar, a quote about transformation, or a grid of platform pillars. Those are habits from a different sale. This buyer wants the artifact. Social proof can follow, and only if it names a technical constraint. "Cut a class of flaky tests in a monorepo" is a start. "Loved by modern teams" is not.

Do not autoplay a product film over the snippet. Let them read. Offer a short recording below if it shows the same real screen. Motion that delays the command is a tax.

Do not ask for a work email before they have seen the tool work. If you must gate a long-lived token, gate that token, not the first screenshot. The screenshot is the invitation. The account is a later commitment.

When the first screen can stand up to an engineer, the next question is usually what it costs to keep using it. Read [how to show the shape of the price without hiding the try path](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-developer-tool-company) before you tuck the numbers behind a call.

To see public product interfaces that lead with the job rather than a slogan, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Got Next and Leadly are examples of screens built around a small set of actions. That standard belongs on a tool company's first view too.

## Test it on someone who ships

Ask an engineer who does not work on the tool to open the page on a laptop, then on a phone. Give them ten seconds. Hide it. Ask what the tool does to their code or their system, and how they would try it. If they repeat a slogan, the artifact is too quiet. If they describe the job and cannot find the install, the action is too quiet.

Stay in the room for a second test. Let them try. Count the steps to a result. If the result is a sales email, the homepage lied. Change the path until a stranger can produce the tool's real output without you narrating.

Read the headline with the picture covered, then the picture with the headline covered. Each should still point at the same job. If they diverge, you have two messages. Keep the one the tool can prove today.
